issue.issue_text: Whether the trial was vitiated for want of a valid and legal sanction for prosecution.

facts: The appellant argued that the sanction to prosecute was invalid.
The sanction was given by a new Chairman of the Kharagpore Municipality who was elected after the Municipality had passed a resolution authorizing its Chairman to grant such sanctions.
The appellant contended that the authorization did not extend to the new Chairman and that the sanction was not granted by the local authority (the Municipality) itself.
law: The Court referred to Section 15(2) of the Bengal Municipal Act.
Under this Act, a Municipality is a 'body corporate' and has 'perpetual succession'.
application: The Court, agreeing with the High Court, reasoned that because the Municipality is a body with perpetual succession, any authorization it grants is not limited to the Chairman in office at that specific time.
The authorization continues to be valid for subsequent Chairmen unless it is formally rescinded by the Municipality.

The Court also rejected the appellant's attempt to introduce a subsequent resolution as new evidence, noting it was passed after the sanction was given and did not invalidate the previous authorization.
Therefore, the new Chairman could validly use the existing authorization to grant the sanction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's challenge, holding that the sanction was valid and legal because the Municipality's authorization to its Chairman was continuous due to its status as a body with perpetual succession. Consequently, the trial was not vitiated.

issue.issue_text: Whether additional evidence, specifically a subsequent resolution by the Municipality, could be adduced to challenge the validity of the original sanction.

facts: The appellant sought permission to introduce additional evidence.
The evidence was a resolution passed by the Kharagpore Municipality on August 18, 1965.
This resolution was passed after the sanction to prosecute the appellant had already been granted.
The appellant's goal was to use this new resolution to argue that the original authorization for the sanction was invalid.
law: Under Section 15(2) of the Bengal Municipal Act, a Municipality is a body corporate with perpetual succession.

An authorization granted by such a body is not limited to the specific officeholder (e.g., the Chairman) at the time but continues in effect for subsequent officeholders unless it is formally rescinded.
application: The Court first noted that the appellant had not made a sufficient legal case to justify adducing fresh evidence at this stage.
It then pointed out that the new resolution was passed after the sanction for prosecution was given, making it irrelevant to the validity of the sanction at the time it was granted.
The Court observed that the new resolution was in similar terms to the original one and did not in any way indicate that the previous authorization was invalid.
The Court suggested that the new resolution was likely passed merely "by way of abundant caution" in response to the legal challenges raised by the appellant during the trial.

Finally, the Court affirmed the High Court's reasoning that the original authorization was continuous and valid for any sitting Chairman due to the Municipality's status as a body with perpetual succession.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the request to adduce the additional evidence, finding that the appellant had not made a proper case for it and that the subsequent resolution was irrelevant, untimely, and did not invalidate the original, legally sound sanction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When standards of quality for articles of food are fixed under the rules of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, any person who deals in articles of food that do not conform to those standards contravenes the provisions of the Act and is liable for punishment.
obiter: Under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, courts may have the discretion to award a lesser sentence than the prescribed minimum if there are adequate and special reasons to do so.
